title: What If We Rammed an Asteroid to Move It? NASA Did, and It Worked Too Well

scenes.text: What if we crashed a spacecraft into an asteroid to push it? NASA tried. It overshot.
September 2022. A 1,200-pound probe called DART hits the asteroid Dimorphos, 7 million miles away, at 14,000 miles an hour.
Dimorphos is 500 feet wide and circles a bigger asteroid every 11 hours 55 minutes. Success meant cutting that by 73 seconds.
Two weeks later, telescopes had the answer: 11 hours 23 minutes. Thirty-two minutes shorter. Twenty-five times the goal.
The hit blasted out over 20 million pounds of rock, and that spray pushed the asteroid harder than the probe itself.
So yes, a probe lighter than a small car can move a mountain. Europe's Hera mission is heading there to see the crater.

description:
What if we rammed an asteroid to change its path? On 26 September 2022 NASA's DART spacecraft, about 1,200 pounds, hit the 500-foot asteroid Dimorphos at roughly 14,000 mph, 7 million miles from Earth.
Dimorphos orbited its larger partner Didymos every 11 hours 55 minutes; the mission needed to shorten that by 73 seconds to count as a success. It shortened it by 32 minutes, more than 25 times the goal, partly because the impact threw out over 20 million pounds of rock whose recoil added to the push. ESA's Hera mission is travelling to the asteroid to study the aftermath.
